strengths: Novel and creative application of computational methods to simulate neurodevelopmental disorders, representing the first work to model brain disorders using system-level neural models
Rigorous experimental design with strong controls (e.g., random unit ablation baseline) and comprehensive hyperparameter analysis demonstrating necessity of targeted VWF-selective unit ablation

Clear demonstration of selective impairment in reading (ROAR below dyslexia threshold) while preserving visual reasoning (RAVEN) and sentence comprehension (Kempler), supporting selectivity hypothesis
Well-grounded in established neuroscience literature on the visual word form area and dyslexia mechanisms
Thorough ablation studies examining mask size, perturbation scale, and layer types, with findings that MLP components are critical
Clear and well-organized presentation with informative figures and appropriate technical detail
weaknesses: Significant divergence from human dyslexia phenotype: model exhibits phonological deficits but NOT orthographic deficits, whereas dyslexic humans show both (though phonological may be primary). This substantially undermines validity claims as a dyslexia simulation

Limited model generalization: main results rely heavily on Qwen2-VL-72B; LLaVA-NeXT showed poor RAVEN baseline (16.67%) preventing selectivity assessment, and PixTral receives minimal analysis. Only two validated models limit confidence in generalizability

Biological validity of identified units not adequately established: VWF-selective units are located in language decoder MLP layers rather than multimodal fusion regions. Unclear why these are 'visual word form' selective versus general word processing units

Insufficient human validation: no direct testing of dyslexic participants on identical benchmarks; human comparison data from different studies; no systematic analysis of error patterns compared to actual dyslexic individuals

Questionable appropriateness of adapted benchmarks: ROAR evaluation ignores response time (key component); Kempler significantly adapted to VQA format; RAVEN uses only 12 items; dyslexia threshold (65%) set somewhat arbitrarily

Limited biological grounding validation: authors acknowledge inability to directly measure neural alignment as 'human data for certain tasks and brain recordings of the VWFA were not accessible'—a critical limitation for claiming functional correspondence
Overstated causality claims: presented as testing 'causal hypotheses' but is an in silico simulation; unclear how findings transfer to understanding human dyslexia mechanisms
Limited practical impact and follow-through: paper promises insights for intervention design and biomarker discovery but provides minimal concrete applications or evidence
Incomplete error analysis: error pattern tables presented qualitatively without systematic comparison to human dyslexic patterns or statistical breakdowns

strengths: Novel methodological contribution: First work to model brain disorders through targeted VLM ablation, introducing 'digital twins' for computational neuroscience
Well-grounded in neuroscience: Leverages established VWFA-dyslexia theory and uses principled fMRI localizer paradigms for identifying task-selective units

Comprehensive evaluation: Multiple standardized benchmarks (ROAR, RAVEN, Kempler, lexical decision) adapted from human clinical assessments, with strong control experiments (random ablation, layer-type analysis, multiple architectures)
Human-model correspondence: Selective phonological (not orthographic) deficits match dyslexic patterns, and importantly the model produces this despite lacking auditory input
Rigorous experimental design: Results averaged over 20 seeds, appropriate statistical testing, good ablation specificity controls, sensitivity analyses for hyperparameters
Clear presentation: Excellent figures, well-written, methods clearly described, reproducibility prioritized (code promised, statistical details provided)
weaknesses: Model-biology validation gap: Identified VWF-selective units never compared against fMRI data from human VWFA; no confirmation that MLP selectivity relates to biological word-selective neurons

Incomplete human matching: Model shows 8% phonological deficit but 0% orthographic, while humans show both (~9% and ~6%); explanation for this mismatch is incomplete and raises questions about model fidelity
Circular threshold selection: Uses human-derived 65% ROAR dyslexia threshold to determine model ablation magnitude—applies human standard to model without validation that this is appropriate
Causality overclaimed: Presented as testing 'causal hypotheses' but work is fundamentally correlational; showing what happens upon ablation differs from proving causation in human brain

Limited mechanistic insight: Core finding (ablating word-selective units impairs word recognition) is somewhat tautological; does not explain how deficits arise or provide deep mechanistic understanding
Benchmark design limitations: Only 12 RAVEN items is small; 50+50 ROAR test items limited; Kempler adapted to VQA changes original task structure; some adaptation choices appear arbitrary
Incomplete model generalization: Main analysis on single model (Qwen2-VL); LLaVA-NeXT showed poor RAVEN baseline (below chance); only PixTral fully replicated—generalizability unclear
Developmental disorder limitation: Captures 'end-state consequences' not developmental trajectories; dyslexia fundamentally emerges during literacy acquisition, not modeled here

Perturbation discontinuity: Only full ablation produces selective effects; other scaling factors produce incoherent outputs or no effect, suggesting discontinuous regime that raises interpretability concerns

Missing error pattern validation: Error types (gibberish, contextual over-interpretation, hedging) shown in Tables 1-3 but unclear if they match human dyslexic errors or reflect model-specific degradation

strengths: Novel and creative framework: First systematic approach to modeling brain disorders through selective unit ablation in VLMs, establishing a generalizable methodology applicable beyond dyslexia

Rigorous methodology with multiple controls: Principled application of neuroscience localizers, systematic layer-type investigation, appropriate random/non-selective layer controls, and clear ablation criteria grounded in epidemiology

Impressive empirical match to human dyslexia: Achieves key dissociation (reading impaired, visual reasoning preserved), selective phonological deficits, font sensitivity patterns, and enhanced non-reading performance—all matching human data

Comprehensive and well-designed evaluation: Multiple reading benchmarks (ROAR, phonological/orthographic dissociation), multiple control tasks (RAVEN, Kempler), fMRI alignment analysis, and font sensitivity testing

Exceptional reproducibility and generalization: Code promised, complete methodology and prompts provided, 20 random seeds with statistical testing, generalization demonstrated across three different VLMs (Qwen2, Molmo, PixTral)
Strong technical soundness: Appropriate statistical testing with confidence intervals, one-tailed t-tests justified by directional hypotheses, clear computational specifications (2× A100 GPUs)

Significant impact potential: Opens new research direction using neural networks as proxies for brain disorders; framework generalizable to psychiatric conditions, brain lesions, and other neurodevelopmental disorders
weaknesses: Limited mechanistic understanding: Paper doesn't explain why VWF ablation produces phonological (not orthographic) deficits or what deep computational principles correspond to human neural constraints; lack of interpretability analysis of what selected units actually encode beyond word-selectivity

Imperfect empirical match with humans: Model shows phonological deficit (−8%) but orthography unaffected (p=0.059), whereas humans show both phonological (−9%) and orthographic (−6%) deficits; paper post-hoc attributes discrepancy to unmeasured comorbidities, weakening claimed correspondence

Causality claims exceed evidence: Frames work as 'testing causal hypotheses' but tests only one specific model; showing ablation impairs reading in VLM does not prove VWFA abnormality is causal in humans; neuroscience literature debates causality, but conclusions don't adequately reflect this uncertainty

Biological validity concerns: Unclear how mechanisms producing reading deficits in VLMs without auditory processing correspond to human brain mechanisms; phonological deficits in non-auditory system require deeper justification and interpretability analysis

Arbitrary design choices with insufficient sensitivity analysis: 65% dyslexia threshold chosen but limited justification for this specific value; no systematic analysis of how results depend on threshold choice; similar issues with k% selection and layer-type choices

Limited scope of evaluation benchmarks: ROAR uses only 100 test items (50+50); Kempler adapted from spoken comprehension to image VQA (changes cognitive demands); no reaction time/fluency measurement despite importance in original ROAR; missing other dyslexia measures (rapid naming, reading fluency over time)

Phonological deficit paradox underexplored: System lacks phonological representations yet exhibits 'phonological' deficits—could reflect orthographic confusion rather than true phonological impairment; fundamental interpretability question deserves deeper analysis

Human comparison data limitations: Luke et al. dataset doesn't report comorbidities; data collection methods differ from models; dyslexic sample demographics/severity not specified; font analysis lacks validation against actual dyslexic readers

Incomplete ablation studies: Gradual degradation not explored; random unit ratios limited to equal numbers; self-attention layers show inverse patterns (Fig. 11) but unexplored; unclear whether effects are MLP-specific or MLP gate projections specifically

Generalizability questions: All tested models are large (12B-72B) with strong OCR; unclear if methodology transfers to smaller models, non-OCR models, or different architectures; all share Transformer architecture

strengths: Novel methodology that creatively adapts neuroscience-inspired functional localization methods to identify and causally manipulate VLM representations
Rigorous experimental design with appropriate controls (VWF-selective vs. random ablations), multiple random seeds (n=20), and proper statistical testing across multiple benchmarks

Comprehensive evaluation using multi-faceted tasks (ROAR, RAVEN, Kempler, phonology/orthography dissociation, font sensitivity) that demonstrate both selective reading deficits and preserved visual reasoning
Strong empirical results showing 32% normalized performance drop on reading tasks while preserving general visual intelligence, with generalization across three different VLM architectures
Neural validation through fMRI alignment analysis demonstrating that identified VWF-selective units correspond to human VWFA activity patterns
Practical applications demonstrated through font sensitivity predictions that align with dyslexia-friendly design principles and human user experience
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, detailed methodology, and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Opens a generalizable computational framework potentially applicable to investigating other brain disorders beyond dyslexia
weaknesses: Conceptual gap inadequately addressed: the analogy between ablating VLM units and VWFA hypoactivation, while suggestive, lacks strong biological justification given fundamental differences in computational mechanisms between VLMs and biological brains

Unexplained finding that phonological deficits emerge from visual disruption despite the model never processing auditory input or phonology developmentally, raising questions about whether this mechanism parallels human dyslexia

Circularities in experimental design: dyslexia threshold (65% ROAR) is based on human population statistics without demonstrating equivalent difficulty across modalities; no sensitivity analysis of threshold dependence
Incomplete comparison with human data: orthographic processing discrepancy (Figure 6c) explained speculatively; only one human dataset (Luke et al., 2023) used for phonology/orthography dissociation
Limited evaluation scope: only 100 test items for ROAR, only 3 large-scale models tested (unclear generalization), and English-only tasks despite dyslexia's cross-linguistic relevance

fMRI alignment effects diminish substantially above 1.25% subset size due to feature correlation, and effect sizes at small percentages are non-trivial but modest, raising questions about the strength of neural correspondence
Key finding under-explored: why do only MLP gate projection layers show reading-selective deficits? Why not attention layers? Mechanistic understanding lacking

Overstated framing: paper claims to 'model dyslexia' and 'establish a framework for investigating brain disorders' but really models one hypothesized mechanism (VWFA hypoactivation) while abstracting away genetic, developmental, and etiological factors
Font validation preliminary: only 12 fonts tested against expert recommendations; no validation against actual dyslexic users to confirm ecological validity
Multiple comparisons across many tests without formal correction, and the Kempler task improvement with ablation (p < 0.01) is interesting but underexplored mechanistically
